props.title: Wuthering Heights

sections.content: Andrea Arnold's raw, visceral adaptation of Wuthering Heights (2011) strips away the costume drama polish typically associated with Brontë adaptations. Unlike the glossy romanticism of Wuthering Heights with Laurence Olivier, Arnold's version emphasizes the brutal naturalism of the Yorkshire moors through handheld cameras and natural lighting. This approach connects thematically to other bold literary adaptations like Jane Eyre (2011) and Bright Star (2009), which similarly prioritize emotional authenticity over period piece conventions.

sections.content: Arnold's decision to cast a black actor (James Howson) as Heathcliff connects to broader conversations about representation in period films, following works like Belle (2013) and The Personal History of David Copperfield (2019). The film's unflinching examination of class, race, and power dynamics recalls other revisionist period pieces like Lady Macbeth (2016), which similarly deconstruct Victorian-era social structures through a contemporary lens.

The film's raw cinematography by Robbie Ryan, featuring extreme close-ups and handheld tracking shots, creates an immersive experience that influenced later literary adaptations like Far from the Madding Crowd (2015) and Lady Macbeth (2016). This visual style emphasizes the physical and emotional brutality of the source material in ways that more traditional adaptations like Pride and Prejudice (2005) deliberately avoid. sections.content: Arnold's Wuthering Heights represents a significant shift in how classic literature can be adapted for modern audiences, following the path blazed by Atonement (2007) and The Duchess (2008). By emphasizing naturalistic performances and visceral filmmaking over traditional costume drama conventions, the film connects to contemporary discussions about class, race, and gender in ways that resonate with films like The Favourite (2018) and Portrait of a Lady on Fire (2019).
